llm.summary: This is a clearly disclosed dLazy image-generation skill that uses a third-party CLI, API key, and cloud uploads in ways that match its stated purpose.

dimensions.detail: The skill's stated purpose is Nano Banana 2.0 image generation and editing; its commands, prompt handling, optional image inputs, API endpoints, and generated output URLs all fit that purpose.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: The trigger keywords include generic image-generation phrases, which could cause accidental activation, but the runtime instructions remain tied to normal dLazy image-generation, authentication, and billing-error workflows.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The artifact contains only Markdown instructions and declares use of the external npm package @dlazy/cli pinned to 1.0.9, with both global install and npx options disclosed.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: Sending prompts and user-selected local media files to api.dlazy.com and files.dlazy.com is proportionate for a hosted image-generation service and is explicitly described.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill discloses that dLazy authentication can store an API key in ~/.dlazy/config.json, with an environment-variable alternative for per-invocation use.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: Install only if you trust dLazy and the pinned @dlazy/cli package. Expect prompts and any local image paths you provide to be sent to dLazy services, and expect the CLI to use or store a dLazy API key that may consume account credits.
llm.findings:
[SQP-1] expected: The broad English trigger terms are real activation-scope noise, but they are still image-generation terms and do not add hidden, unrelated, destructive, or deceptive behavior.
[SQP-1] expected: The Chinese trigger terms raise the same accidental-invocation concern; this should be handled with user confirmation before uploads or paid API calls, not by treating the artifact as malicious or requiring Review.
